decks.domain: Turns and intersections: signals, turning lanes, U-turns, right of way and roundabouts

cards.front: Which moves require a signal, and what do you check before making any of them?
cards.back: A signal is required before you turn, change lanes, leave a roundabout or pull away from a curb, and before any of these moves you check ahead, behind and to the side that it is safe.

cards.front: When you are moving in traffic, how far ahead must your turn signal go on?
cards.back: When you are moving in traffic, your turn signal must go on at least one hundred feet before the turn or lane change.

cards.front: How long do you signal when pulling away from a curb into traffic?
cards.back: Pulling away from a curb into traffic, keep your signal on long enough that drivers know you are coming into the lane.

cards.front: How does the signal rule differ when moving in traffic versus leaving a curb?
cards.back: The one hundred-foot signal rule applies when you are already moving in traffic, while leaving a curb you signal long enough to warn traffic rather than for a set distance.

cards.front: When may hand-and-arm signals be used, and what must you use at night?
cards.back: Hand-and-arm signals may be used only in daylight when you can clearly see people and vehicles one thousand feet away; at night or in poor visibility you must use your signal lights.

cards.front: What vehicles should you never use hand-and-arm signals in?
cards.back: Do not use hand-and-arm signals while driving a wide or long vehicle.

cards.front: Which hand-and-arm signals does the manual show?
cards.back: The manual shows three hand-and-arm signals: one for a right turn, one for a left turn and one for stopping or slowing down.

cards.front: How do signal lights and hand signals differ in when they may be used?
cards.back: Signal lights work at any time, but hand-and-arm signals are limited to daylight with a clear view of one thousand feet, so darkness or poor visibility means lights only.

cards.front: Why should you not depend only on another driver's turn signal?
cards.back: Never rely only on another driver's turn signal, because that driver may turn the other way or turn without signaling at all.

decks.module: Safe turns around bikes and walkers
decks.domain: Turns and intersections: signals, turning lanes, U-turns, right of way and roundabouts

cards.front: Do turning rules apply only at intersections?
cards.back: Turning rules apply wherever you turn, including driveways and alleys, not just at intersections.

cards.front: What should you do well before a turn, and how should the turn itself be made?
cards.back: Check for traffic behind and beside you well before you turn, then make the turn smoothly at a lower speed.

cards.front: What is the general rule for which lane you turn from and into?
cards.back: The general turning rule is to go from the nearest lane in your direction of travel into the nearest lane in the direction you want to go, without swinging wide or changing lanes during the turn.

cards.front: What two turning errors does the manual picture?
cards.back: The manual pictures two turning errors: turning into the wrong lane and turning from the wrong lane.
cards.memory_hook: wrong lane in, wrong lane out

cards.front: What may and may not a driver do with a bicycle lane when turning?
cards.back: You may cross a bicycle lane to make a turn, but you must not pull into the bike lane to get ready for the turn.

cards.front: What is the difference between crossing a bike lane and entering it before a turn?
cards.back: Crossing a bike lane during a turn is allowed, but merging into the bike lane ahead of the turn is not.

cards.front: Why do you check mirrors and look over your shoulder before turning?
cards.back: Before turning, check mirrors and look over your shoulder for bicyclists in your blind spot, since riders can come up beside you while you prepare to turn.

cards.front: When turning, who must you yield to and stop for?
cards.back: When turning you must yield to bicyclists in a bike lane or on a sidewalk, and you check the crosswalk and stop for pedestrians.

cards.front: What should you do if you reach an intersection in the wrong lane for your turn?
cards.back: If you arrive at an intersection in the wrong lane for your turn, go on to the next intersection, because circling the block is safer than a last-second lane or direction change.

decks.domain: Turns and intersections: signals, turning lanes, U-turns, right of way and roundabouts

cards.front: Where do you position for a right turn, and what is the scan just before the intersection?
cards.back: For a right turn, move as close as you can to the right curb or road edge, and just before entering the intersection look left, ahead, right and left again.

cards.front: Which lane do you use for a left turn on a two-way road, and who must you yield to?
cards.back: For a left turn on a two-way road, approach in the lane just right of the center line, and Oregon law requires you to yield to oncoming traffic until the turn is safe.

cards.front: How do the starting positions for right and left turns on a two-way road differ?
cards.back: A right turn starts as close as possible to the right curb or road edge, while a left turn on a two-way road starts in the lane just right of the center line.
cards.memory_hook: curb for right, center for left

cards.front: Does the head check before a left turn differ from the one before a right turn?
cards.back: Before a right turn and before a left turn the same head check applies: left, ahead, right, then left again.

cards.front: Where should a left turn begin and where should it end?
cards.back: Make a left turn just before the imaginary center point of the intersection and finish just to the right of the center line of the new street.

cards.front: What are the rules about a left turn on red onto a two-way road and about left turn lanes?
cards.back: Turning left onto a two-way road against a red light is illegal, and where a left turn lane is provided you must turn from that lane.

cards.front: When may two or more lanes turn the same way at the same time?
cards.back: Two or more lanes may turn the same way at once only where lane use signs or pavement markings allow it, and each driver follows the markings and stays in their own lane through the turn.

cards.front: Turning left from a one-way road onto another one-way road, which lanes do you use and is red allowed?
cards.back: Turning left from a one-way road onto another one-way road, approach in the lane nearest the left curb and turn into the nearest left lane; this turn is allowed on red after you stop and yield to traffic and pedestrians.

cards.front: Turning from a two-way road onto a one-way road, which lanes do you use and is red allowed?
cards.back: Turning from a two-way road onto a one-way road, approach in the lane nearest the side you are turning toward and turn into the nearest lane; this turn is also allowed on red after stopping and yielding.

cards.front: Turning left from a one-way road onto a two-way road, which lanes do you use and is red allowed?
cards.back: Turning left from a one-way road onto a two-way road, approach in the lane nearest the left curb and turn into the lane just right of the center line; this turn may not be made on a red light.

cards.front: How does the red-light rule differ for a one-way road's left turn onto a one-way versus a two-way road?
cards.back: A left turn from one one-way road onto another is allowed on red after a stop and yield, but a left turn from a one-way road onto a two-way road is never allowed on red.

cards.front: How does a turn from a two-way onto a one-way road compare with a left onto a two-way road on red?
cards.back: Turning from a two-way road onto a one-way road may be made against a red light after stopping and yielding, the opposite of a left turn onto a two-way road on red.

cards.front: Leaving a one-way road to turn left, what stays the same and what changes with the new road?
cards.back: Leaving a one-way road to turn left, you start from the lane nearest the left curb whether the new road is one-way or two-way; only the lane you end in changes.

decks.domain: Turns and intersections: signals, turning lanes, U-turns, right of way and roundabouts

cards.front: Can you make a U-turn at an intersection with a traffic signal?
cards.back: U-turns are banned at intersections controlled by a traffic signal unless a sign allows the turn.

cards.front: Can you make a U-turn between intersections in a city?
cards.back: U-turns are banned between intersections in a city.

cards.front: How does the U-turn ban at a signal intersection differ from the ban between city intersections?
cards.back: A U-turn at a signal-controlled intersection is banned unless a sign allows it, whereas a U-turn between intersections in a city is banned outright.

cards.front: Inside city limits, how far away must approaching traffic be able to see you for a U-turn?
cards.back: Inside city limits, a U-turn is banned anywhere traffic coming from either direction cannot see your vehicle within five hundred feet.

cards.front: Outside city limits, how far away must approaching traffic be able to see you for a U-turn?
cards.back: Outside city limits, a U-turn is banned anywhere traffic coming from either direction cannot see your vehicle within one thousand feet.

cards.front: How do the U-turn visibility distances compare inside and outside city limits?
cards.back: The U-turn visibility distance is five hundred feet inside city limits but one thousand feet outside city limits.

cards.front: Besides intersections and visibility limits, where else are U-turns banned?
cards.back: U-turns are banned at or on a railroad crossing and anywhere official signs or markings prohibit them.

decks.domain: Turns and intersections: signals, turning lanes, U-turns, right of way and roundabouts

cards.front: What does a defensive driver never assume about stop signs and signals?
cards.back: A defensive driver never assumes that a stop sign or traffic signal will make approaching traffic stop.

cards.front: Where do you stop at a stop sign or a red light?
cards.back: At a stop sign, a steady red signal or a flashing red signal, stop before the marked stop line or crosswalk, or if neither is marked, before the unmarked crossing area.

cards.front: Making an allowed turn, who must you always yield to?
cards.back: Always yield to vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and bicyclists, and to traffic already in the intersection, when making an allowed turn.

cards.front: After stopping, what do you do if you still cannot see cross traffic?
cards.back: If you cannot see traffic coming from the left and right after stopping, pull forward slightly and scan before going on.

cards.front: What must be true before you enter an intersection on a green light?
cards.back: Even with a green light, do not enter an intersection unless your vehicle has room on the far side.

cards.front: Does a green light mean the way through the intersection is clear?
cards.back: A green light lets you go only if there is space for your vehicle beyond the intersection; a green light does not mean the way through is clear.

cards.front: Who goes first at a four-way stop, and who do you yield to when unsure?
cards.back: At a four-way stop, courtesy lets the driver who stopped first go first, and when in doubt you yield to the driver on your right, never assuming others will yield to you.

cards.front: Where two-way stop signs face each other, who yields?
cards.back: Where two-way stop signs face each other, a driver turning left yields to approaching or oncoming traffic going straight.

cards.front: How do the four-way stop and the facing two-way stop differ on who goes first?
cards.back: At a four-way stop the first driver to stop goes first by courtesy, while at a two-way stop with facing signs the driver turning left yields to oncoming straight traffic.

cards.front: At an intersection with no signs or signals, how do you scan and who do you yield to?
cards.back: At an intersection with no signs or signals, look left first to see that cross traffic is yielding, then ahead and right, and yield to any vehicle already in the intersection or coming from your right.

cards.front: When your road ends at an uncontrolled T intersection, who has the right of way?
cards.back: When your road dead-ends into an uncontrolled T intersection, drivers on the through road have the right of way and you must yield to them.

cards.front: How do uncontrolled crossroads and uncontrolled T intersections differ on who yields?
cards.back: At an uncontrolled intersection you yield to vehicles already in it or coming from the right, while at an uncontrolled T intersection the driver on the ending road yields to through traffic.

decks.domain: Turns and intersections: signals, turning lanes, U-turns, right of way and roundabouts

cards.front: What are roundabouts, and which direction does traffic move in them?
cards.back: Roundabouts, rotaries and traffic circles are circular intersections with a center island, and traffic always moves counterclockwise around it.

cards.front: What does a warning sign with arrows in a circle tell you?
cards.back: A warning sign showing arrows in a circle tells you a circular intersection is ahead.

cards.front: What should you do as you approach a roundabout?
cards.back: Approaching a roundabout, slow down, read the signs to find your exit, watch for bicyclists who may merge or use the sidewalk, and stop for pedestrians in the crosswalk in your lane.

cards.front: How do you enter a roundabout?
cards.back: To enter a roundabout you yield to traffic already inside and to traffic exiting, wait for a gap, merge, and stay ready to stop.

cards.front: Inside a roundabout, how do you treat a bicyclist who has merged into traffic?
cards.back: Inside a roundabout, circle until your exit, give a bicyclist who has merged into traffic the full lane, and never pass a bicyclist within the roundabout.

cards.front: What choices does a bicyclist have at a roundabout, and what does a merging rider get?
cards.back: A bicyclist approaching a roundabout may either merge with traffic or use the sidewalk, and one who merges gets the full travel lane with no passing inside.

cards.front: What do you do when leaving a roundabout?
cards.back: To leave a roundabout, use your right turn signal and watch for pedestrians in the crosswalk, ready to stop.

cards.front: How do your duties differ when entering and leaving a roundabout?
cards.back: Entering a roundabout you yield to circulating and exiting traffic, while leaving it you give a right turn signal and watch the crosswalk.

cards.front: How do you handle lanes in a multi-lane roundabout?
cards.back: In a multi-lane roundabout, read exit and lane use signs and markings before entering, pick the lane for your exit, keep that lane until you leave and avoid lane changes inside.

cards.front: In a multi-lane roundabout, when do you choose your lane?
cards.back: In a multi-lane roundabout you choose the lane for your exit before entering and hold it, rather than changing lanes once inside.

cards.front: How should you treat a truck inside a roundabout?
cards.back: Trucks may straddle both lanes of a roundabout, and passing or driving beside a truck inside a roundabout is illegal.

cards.front: What do you do if an emergency vehicle approaches before you enter a roundabout?
cards.back: When emergency vehicles are approaching, do not enter the roundabout; pull to the right and let other vehicles clear the intersection.

cards.front: What do you do if an emergency vehicle approaches while you are inside a roundabout?
cards.back: Never stop inside a roundabout for an emergency vehicle; keep going, exit, and then pull onto the right shoulder to let it pass.

cards.front: How does your response to an emergency vehicle differ outside and inside a roundabout?
cards.back: For an emergency vehicle outside a roundabout you stay out and pull right, but once inside you keep moving, exit and then pull over; stopping in the circle is never correct.

recap_hooks.text: Every turn, lane change, curb pull or roundabout exit gets a signal and a look all around first.
Arm signals belong to clear daylight in ordinary vehicles, and another driver's blinker is only a hint.

recaps.module: Safe turns around bikes and walkers

recap_hooks.text: Turn from the nearest lane into the nearest lane, crossing a bike lane but never riding in it.
Riders and walkers come first, and a wrong lane means the next intersection, not a swerve.
Right turns hug the curb, left turns start beside the center line, and both use the same head check.
Red allows a turn into a one-way road after a stop, but never a left onto a two-way road.
No U-turns at signals without a sign, mid-block in a city, or on railroad tracks.
Approaching drivers must see you within five hundred feet in town and one thousand feet outside it.
Never trust a sign to stop others, and on green go only with room beyond.
First to stop goes first, left turners wait at facing stops, and the through road wins at a T.
Yield on the way in, circle counterclockwise, and signal right on the way out.
Pick your lane early, never pass trucks or merged riders inside, and never stop in the circle for an emergency vehicle.
